title: GlusterFS Networking Explained: Why Port 24007 Alone Is Not Enough
summary: GlusterFS clients use discovery first and connect directly to brick processes afterward. Learn which traffic must be reachable and why this matters especially in Kubernetes.
author: Eliware
content:
# GlusterFS Networking Explained: Why Port 24007 Alone Is Not Enough

One of the most common GlusterFS networking mistakes is treating the management or discovery port as if it carries all storage traffic. It does not.

A client may successfully contact a GlusterFS server, discover a volume, and still fail to mount or use that volume because it cannot reach the brick processes that actually serve the data.

The short version is:

```text
Discovery gets the client the map.
Brick connections move the data.
```

Understanding that distinction is essential on ordinary Linux networks and even more important in Kubernetes, where a Service, pod address, or load balancer can make one part of the path look healthy while another part remains unreachable.

## The two stages of a GlusterFS connection

A native GlusterFS client does not simply send every read and write to the hostname used in the mount command. The connection has two broad stages.

### 1. Discovery

The client contacts a GlusterFS server and asks for the volume configuration. That configuration identifies the volume, its bricks, and the client-side translators needed to route file operations.

This is the job of the Gluster management service, commonly associated with TCP port `24007`. The address used for discovery can be any suitable GlusterFS server address that the client can reach.

### 2. Direct brick traffic

After discovery, the native client connects directly to the brick processes listed in the volume configuration. Reads, writes, metadata operations, and replica coordination depend on these connections.

Those brick processes use their own TCP ports. In many installations the ports are assigned from a configured range beginning at `49152`. The exact range depends on the server configuration, so operators should inspect and document the range used by their deployment.

The important property is not a particular port number. It is that the advertised brick addresses and ports must be directly reachable from the client.

## Why opening 24007 can still produce a broken mount

Imagine a client and three storage nodes behind a firewall. The firewall allows TCP `24007` to one node, so the client receives a valid volume configuration. But the firewall blocks the brick ports or the advertised node addresses are only routable inside the storage network.

The discovery step succeeds. The data path fails.

Depending on the exact failure, the client may report a mount error, a transport endpoint error, stalled operations, or a volume that appears mounted but cannot reliably perform I/O. Looking only at the discovery port can send troubleshooting in the wrong direction.

The official GlusterFS client documentation describes this behavior: after contacting the server, the client communicates with the individual brick processes. It also notes that one port is required for each brick, beginning at the configured brick-port range. See the [official client setup guide](https://docs.gluster.org/en/latest/Administrator-Guide/Setting-Up-Clients/).

## A useful traffic diagram

For a three-brick replica volume, think of the connection like this:

```text
                         discovery
                    TCP 24007
                         │
                         ▼
                  ┌─────────────┐
                  │ Gluster node │
                  │ returns map  │
                  └──────┬──────┘
                         │
        ┌────────────────┼────────────────┐
        │                │                │
        ▼                ▼                ▼
  node 1 brick      node 2 brick      node 3 brick
  TCP 49152+       TCP 49152+       TCP 49152+
        │                │                │
        └──────────── direct storage traffic ────────┘
```

The discovery endpoint is not a general-purpose proxy for those final connections. A load balancer that selects one GlusterFS node for discovery cannot automatically proxy the client’s subsequent brick connections unless the entire deployment has been deliberately designed and validated for that behavior.

## Kubernetes adds another layer of risk

Kubernetes makes it easy to create a stable Service name, but a stable name does not guarantee that every address returned to a GlusterFS client is useful to that client.

There are several separate questions to answer:

- Can the client resolve the discovery hostname?
- Can it reach the discovery port?
- What addresses does the GlusterFS server advertise for its bricks?
- Can the client route to each advertised address?
- Are the brick ports allowed by NetworkPolicy, firewalls, and cloud security groups?
- Will those addresses remain valid after pod recreation?
- Does the client network differ from the network used by the GlusterFS pods?

A Service can answer the first two questions while leaving the others unresolved. This is why GlusterFS networking must be designed around the full advertised topology, not just the first hostname in a mount command.

## The Eliware topology

The Eliware storage design keeps discovery traffic and direct brick traffic separate. The current image uses:

- TCP `24007` for GlusterFS discovery; and
- TCP `49152–49157` for the six current brick processes on each node.

In the Kubernetes topology, stable per-node native endpoints are used for the addresses that clients need after discovery. A discovery-only load balancer can select any GlusterFS node for the initial request, but it does not replace the direct paths to the node-local bricks.

That design is more explicit than pretending one virtual IP represents the complete storage network. It also makes the operational requirement visible: Kubernetes pod networking must permit native clients to reach the brick range directly.

The project’s [storage contract](https://glusterfs.eliware.org/) treats this as a hard boundary. Do not route the administrative API publicly, do not access brick paths directly from application pods, and do not assume that discovery connectivity proves data-path connectivity.

## A practical firewall checklist

Before mounting a volume from a client, verify the following.

### On every GlusterFS server

- The management service is running.
- The expected peers are connected.
- The volume is started.
- The brick processes are online.
- The brick-port range is configured and documented.
- The server advertises addresses reachable by the client network.

Useful commands include:

```sh
sudo gluster peer status
sudo gluster volume info testvol
sudo gluster volume status testvol
```

### From the client

- Resolve every discovery and advertised brick hostname.
- Test the discovery port.
- Test the relevant brick ports on every advertised node.
- Confirm that routing uses the intended interface and network.
- Check local firewall logs when a connection is rejected.

For a simple TCP reachability test, use a tool available on your system, such as `nc`:

```sh
nc -vz gluster1 24007
nc -vz gluster1 49152
nc -vz gluster2 49152
nc -vz gluster3 49152
```

A successful check to one brick port is not proof that every brick port is reachable. Test the actual ports reported by the volume status and the range configured for your environment.

## Common designs that cause trouble

### One discovery load balancer, private brick addresses

The client reaches the load balancer, receives private pod or node addresses, and cannot route to them. Discovery succeeds, I/O fails.

### NetworkPolicy allows only the Service port

The policy allows TCP `24007` but denies the brick range. The symptoms resemble a broken volume even though peer discovery looks healthy.

### Brick addresses resolve differently for different clients

A storage node may advertise a hostname that resolves correctly inside the cluster but not from an external Linux client. The mount command can use a reachable name while the returned brick addresses remain unusable.

### Host ports are assumed to equal container ports

Compose, Kubernetes, and host-level firewalls can translate ports differently. Document the client-visible address and port, not just the port inside the container.

### Application pods access brick directories

Brick directories are server-side storage implementation paths. Application clients should mount the GlusterFS volume through the native client or an explicitly validated access layer such as NFS-Ganesha. Reading or writing brick paths directly bypasses GlusterFS coordination and can corrupt the volume.

## Native client versus NFS-Ganesha

The native GlusterFS client and NFS-Ganesha are different access paths. The native client connects to the GlusterFS volume and its bricks. NFS clients connect to the Ganesha service, commonly on TCP `2049`, and Ganesha translates NFS operations to GlusterFS operations through the configured FSAL.

If you enable NFS-Ganesha, validate its own service reachability and failover behavior separately. A healthy GlusterFS brick path does not automatically prove that an NFS export is configured or available. Conversely, an NFS export does not eliminate the need to keep the underlying GlusterFS network healthy.

The Eliware Compose topology leaves NFS disabled by default. That is deliberate: NFS-Ganesha is an optional deployment layer, not something to infer from the presence of GlusterFS packages alone.

## A better troubleshooting order

When a mount fails, work from the lower-level facts upward:

1. Confirm the client can resolve the discovery hostname.
2. Confirm the management service is reachable.
3. Confirm the peer and volume state on the cluster.
4. Inspect the brick addresses and ports returned by the server.
5. Test direct connectivity from the client to every advertised brick.
6. Check NetworkPolicy, host firewalls, security groups, and routing.
7. Confirm the client and server package versions and mount options.
8. Inspect GlusterFS and client logs.
9. Test the mount again only after the data path is confirmed.

This order separates cluster state from network state. It also prevents a common waste of time: repeatedly changing volume options when the client simply cannot reach a brick.

## The rule to remember

If you remember only one thing, remember this:

> GlusterFS discovery tells the client where the volume is. Direct brick connectivity is what lets the client use it.

Design, firewall, and Kubernetes policies around both paths. A replica-3 volume can provide useful availability, but only when clients can reach the storage nodes that hold the replicas.

For a complete first-volume exercise, start with our [EL10 installation and replica-3 guide](https://glusterfs.eliware.org/). For the storage model behind the connection flow, read the official [GlusterFS architecture documentation](https://docs.gluster.org/en/latest/Quick-Start-Guide/Architecture/).
